text: As far as I know, Cassini was designed to run out of fuel while in a high orbit, and if it drifted, Saturn's gravity could fling it onto an icy moon, which is exactly where biologists wanted to protect. I think that's the real reason for the crash: it made the end deliberate instead of a random later impact. Does that matter much? I guess not for a probe with instruments in old condition, but for moon contamination it's much safer to steer it into the planet's atmosphere where it burns up. I'd say a controlled crash was the cautious way to leave things as they were.

I think the stationary leg hurts because it's doing a lot of quiet work even when it isn't the one pushing off. When you ride, your center of mass shifts and the planted leg has to stabilize the board, absorb small impacts from cracks and curbs, and resist sideways forces as you turn. That kind of holding and bracing tires the muscles fast, and if you're gripping or leaning hard, the soreness shows up in the knee or shin. I also suspect your stance has something to do with it. If the stationary foot is too far out to the side, or you're keeping it rigid, the joint takes more strain. I've read that a loose, bent knee stance helps because the leg can absorb shocks instead of transmitting them straight into the bones. I'd say check how you're setting that foot down and whether you're allowing a little flexion in the knee. Does that matter much? Probably not if you're only skating a short distance, but for longer sessions it matters because fatigue makes the hurt worse. A lot of the pain is really just muscle and joint stress from holding the board steady. I'd give the leg a day or two and see if it eases. If it keeps hurting or the spot is sharp and localized, I'd get someone to look at it rather than assume it's normal. Anyway, I don't know your exact setup, so treat this as a general take. To me the big thing is that the stationary leg is still doing the stabilizing work while the other foot controls the board. I guess the hurt is mostly that repeated work plus fatigue, and maybe a slightly stiff or wide stance is making it worse for you.

I think the name is less about where someone was born and more about the ancestral line they inherit. For most Black Americans, the Afro part doesn't mean a current passport or recent migration, it means their family history goes back to Africa. A lot of people in the US have no memory of living there, yet their roots are still African, because generations of their ancestors were carried there or came from there. I guess that's why African American or Afro-American made sense as an identity: it recognizes a shared historical connection without assuming everyone has personally lived in Africa. Of course, some people were born in the US and still identify with it, and I'd say that's normal. The term is more a label for a cultural and racial lineage than a statement that most members actually migrated from Africa recently. I can see why the distinction trips people up. If your grandmother was born in Atlanta but her great-grandparents came from West Africa, you can still be Afro-American in the broader sense. I suppose what matters is whether you claim that ancestry, not whether you have a stamp in your passport.

I’d say a mix of regional suppliers and local black markets. Iran has been a big one, often through Lebanese groups, and neighbours like Lebanon, Iraq and Jordan have also supplied fighters. Militias buy arms from whichever side they fight alongside, and small arms cross borders a lot. As for why it continues, I think because the fighting hasn’t stopped, so each side keeps arming its fighters. I guess it’s less about one big reason and more about a steady stream of smuggling. Does that matter much? Probably not for most people, but it explains why the guns keep coming.

I think the word bad does a lot of work in this question. For me the interesting question isn't whether every drug is bad, but whether intense pleasure has to come with downsides. As far as I know, most of the drugs people mean when they say intense pleasure or euphoria act on the same reward circuits in the brain, and those circuits also handle motivation and learning. That overlap is the real problem. If a substance tells the brain that something very good happened, the brain has to update its expectations about the future, and that update can start to warp ordinary life. I'd say the body and brain can adapt, and the person starts needing the drug to feel normal, which always seemed less dramatic than the movies make it, but still real.

I don't believe all drugs are bad in a moral sense. Some are just boring or risky because of dose or impurities, while others are useful when used carefully. What makes heroines and amphetamines dangerous has more to do with how they hijack the reward system than with the drug molecule alone. A pleasure drug with zero adverse effects would have to avoid that hijacking, which is hard. If pleasure feels the same no matter the source, the brain may still adapt, and then normal life can feel dull. Even if it never produced a physical sickness, the learning part of the brain could still get stuck on a very strong signal. That's the bit people miss. I'd still wonder if it left everyday life feeling less interesting. If you chase a perfect high enough, the ordinary stuff loses some of its pull, and that isn't the same as physical harm, but it's still a cost.

It's tempting to imagine a perfectly safe pleasure drug, and for a short holiday I'd want one too. I guess my complaint is that if it only gives euphoria and never changes how the brain learns or adapts, it's a lot easier to use than people think. Does that matter much? Probably not for most people. My own opinion is that a pleasure drug with zero adverse effects would probably still have an opportunity cost. Time spent chasing it is time not spent building skills and relationships, and that opportunity cost can quietly drain your life even when the drug itself feels harmless. That's probably more than enough to make most people cautious.

Hi Sam,

I get it, and the pain is real, so don't doubt that part. I think it's mostly the combination of standing still for long spells and the tight shoes you'd pick for shopping, plus the fatigue from walking around. For me, the worst part is the tension building up in the neck and shoulders, which can feel like a dull ache that won't quit. I'd say that's why it's different from a normal headache. It's real, but it can feel vague, and it usually fades once you sit down and rest.

Cheers,
Me

I think you said milk because cows are so strongly tied to milk in everyday talk, and if you were dazed or tired, the obvious answer can slip out even when another answer is actually the one they wanted. I've had moments like that too, where something feels instantly right and I'm not sure I can tell if it was a simple lapse or just my brain jumping to the first associated word. The fact that it felt certain doesn't make it more accurate, which always seemed silly to me. I'd guess you weren't thinking hard enough about the trick in the question, and the cow-milk association took over. I mean, if you're not paying attention, you'll just answer the obvious one. Does that matter much? Probably not for most people. It's the sort of little slip that can happen to anyone, and it makes me laugh.

Cheers,

Hi,

I’m glad you asked, because house buying is one of those things people get wrong in small ways that add up later. I think the most important thing is to get pre approved before you start falling in love with a house, since that tells you what you can actually afford and keeps you from chasing places you can’t reach. When you find one you like, get a professional inspection, because minor problems now can become expensive surprises after closing. I’d push on the price if the inspection finds issues, or ask the seller to fix the biggest ones. You should read the contract carefully, or have a solicitor check it, especially the clauses about repair, deposits, and completion. From what I’ve read, comparing mortgage offers matters more than people think. A rate that looks lower can carry fees that eat the savings. For utilities, I’d ask the current owner for recent bills so you aren’t walking into high heating costs or old pipes. I’ve seen people get excited over a property and ignore the neighborhood, parking, and street noise. Those small things affect daily life a lot. I’d rather you move slowly than live with regrets.

Cheers,
Me

Hi,
I think the main difference is the blend of ingredients, and I'd say a 3-in-1 is really just a compromise formula rather than three proper products in one bottle. Shampoo bits need strong surfactants that create lather and remove grease, while conditioner bits need softer agents that leave a film on the hair and skin, and the bodywash part just needs something mild and moisturising. Packing all of that into one liquid means you get a middle of the road product, and that always seemed silly to me for people with dry hair or sensitive skin. Compared with a separate shampoo, a 3-in-1 usually has less cleansing power, and compared with a separate conditioner, the conditioning is weak. A 2-in-1 has to work harder to handle cleaning and conditioning, while a 3-in-1 also has to think about body skin, so the whole thing gets diluted. I've used some and found them fine for everyday washing, but if you have a specific hair or skin problem, I'd just buy the separate bottles. I mean, if you only want one bottle for the whole family, it can be convenient. From what I've read, the formula tends to be more about convenience and price than performance, and I think that's the real difference, not magic. Does that matter much? Probably not for most people, but I do think you lose flexibility.
Cheers,
Me

Hi,

I'd say they do it by putting GPS receivers on bedrock and comparing where the same points sit after years of observation. You don't get a speed instantly, because the motion is tiny, so researchers look at position changes over long periods and divide by time, which gives a velocity in millimetres per year. For the numbers to mean anything you also need a stable reference system, and for that they use satellite laser ranging and very long baseline interferometry to check the GPS data. You need many stations across the continent and you also have to correct for local ground shifts after earthquakes or changes in ice weight.

I guess what surprises people is that even a few millimetres a year adds up fast enough to explain why continents sit where they do now. I've read that some plates creep along at a couple of centimetres a year, which always seemed silly to me until you think about geological time. Does any of that matter much day to day? Probably not, but it is the reason we can track continental drift without needing to see it with our own eyes.

Cheers

I think the main reason is that related parents share genes more often, so their children are more likely to inherit two copies of the same rare or mildly bad mutations. IQ is affected by many genes, not one 'IQ gene,' so when two similar variants meet, the small effects can add up and pull cognitive development down. I'd say this is about recessive genetic risk becoming visible more often in close relatives. The closer the relationship, the higher the chance of those hidden variants becoming active, which is why inbreeding tends to lower measured IQ on average. I guess it's a matter of odds, not a fixed penalty. Some inbred children will be fine, but the group average is lower because more bad combinations are being expressed. As far as I know, this is the same logic behind the inbreeding coefficient, and it tracks how often identical gene copies meet.

When an injury is in the arm, the pain can feel milder than injuries to the torso, groin, or head, and there are several reasons. The arm is an appendage, so the person can hold it close, keep it still, or shield it, which changes how the body registers the injury. Pain perception isn't just about nerve density. The brain can scale pain down when other injuries, fear, or adrenaline grab attention. Injuries near vital organs feel more threatening, and the body responds to that sense of threat. Muscle and tissue in the arm can absorb some impact, but that isn't the whole explanation. In short, an arm injury may seem less painful because the limb can be protected, attention can shift, and the body manages threat. It doesn't mean arm injuries are harmless; they still need proper care. For a new colleague, the practical takeaway is that visible arm pain should still be taken seriously.

The difference comes down to how each gas interacts with blood. Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, which is why even modest breaths over time can matter. When carbon monoxide attaches to hemoglobin, it forms carboxyhemoglobin and takes up the space where oxygen should be. That means less oxygen can be carried to muscles, brain and organs, even when the air still has normal oxygen levels. The binding strength is the central reason. Oxygen's job in red blood cells is to pick up and release oxygen where it is needed. Carbon monoxide gets in there and stays on the hemoglobin long enough to block that exchange. That means symptoms can appear even without a dramatic drop in the oxygen content of the inhaled air.

Carbon dioxide is handled very differently. Our lungs are designed to expel it as a waste product of metabolism. We breathe out carbon dioxide constantly, and healthy ventilation keeps blood levels within a workable range, so at normal indoor concentrations it is not the immediate poison that carbon monoxide is. Carbon dioxide can accumulate in a sealed space, but in normal rooms it is removed by ventilation and breathing out. It is only when levels climb that it becomes a real concern, such as in very closed or crowded spaces. At high levels carbon dioxide does cause problems because it changes blood chemistry and can overwhelm ventilation, but that is a different failure mode from carbon monoxide. The practical point for a new colleague is that carbon monoxide is a quiet hazard. It has no strong smell and is invisible, so people can be exposed for a while before feeling short of breath, getting a headache or feeling dizzy.

The brace position is what you're asked to use if a crash is likely. I think the main idea is simple: when the plane decelerates or hits something, your body keeps moving forward, and the brace lets you use the seat and your own posture to absorb that motion. You put your feet flat on the floor, bend forward, keep your chin tucked, and hold the seat or cover your head, depending on the instruction. From what I've read, this helps stop your head and torso from being thrown into the seatback or cabin, which is a common source of injury. I'd say the position is a way of turning your body into a controlled stopping system rather than letting inertia do the work. It also helps keep the airway open, which matters if you have to keep breathing while the cabin is chaotic. For most passengers, I guess the details will be explained in-flight, but the basic idea is that you brace with your body close to the seat, hands and head protected, feet planted. I mean, it's one of those safety steps that looks fussy, but I think it can make a real difference in a sudden stop. That much seemed reasonable to me.

Hi. I can see why you'd ask that. I think the names of very old businesses usually got lost, or the companies got absorbed into newer ones. Does that matter much? Probably not for most people, but the names and records often didn't survive well. The industrial era changed how people bought and sold things, and it's when the kinds of companies people know today really began. Most recognizable brands started after that shift, which makes them much younger than the factories we might picture. I'd say it's less that they never existed and more that they didn't stick around.

I think the lower rate at the dealership is mostly a surface thing, and if you only look at the APR you're likely to end up paying more overall. The reason bank financing can come out cheaper is that dealers often load the loan with extras that don't show up in the rate. I've seen quotes where the advertised rate looked great, but the payment included extended warranty, prepaid maintenance, paint protection, doc fees and other add-ons. Once those extra costs are counted, the effective cost of borrowing can be higher than a plain bank loan.

A bank usually offers a simpler product. You ask for a car loan, get a number, and pay it off without a salesperson pushing you into bundles. That simplicity matters. Dealers can quote low APR because car makers often pay them to steer customers to their financing or leasing desk. The lower rate is a sales incentive, not a guarantee of a better deal. I'd say the real comparison should be total cost, not the rate alone.

What does that mean in practice? A dealer's sticker might include a mandatory protection package and a preparation fee, while a bank might quote a higher rate but with no add-ons. If those dealer extras add a few hundred or a few thousand dollars, the bank can end up cheaper despite the higher nominal rate. I've also noticed that dealer financing can lock you into their service centre or require insurance through them, which makes switching later more awkward.

Take the bank quote and ask the dealer to put their full cost in writing. Compare the total amount you would pay over the life of the loan, including every fee and add-on. That is where the dealer's lower rate can hide behind the fine print. I would not trust the headline APR by itself, because it does not tell you what is bundled into the payment.

For me, the cheaper option is often the bank, and the reason is what the dealer charges around the loan. I'd ask for the total loan cost and every optional product priced out. If the dealer total is still lower than the bank after all fees, then the dealership might win. But from what I've read and the quotes I've seen, the bank frequently comes out ahead when you count everything.

I keep thinking about how strange it is that cannabis remains federally illegal while legal in many US states. I don't think one national law would fix everything, and the state-by-state confusion is less painful than the headlines suggest. Colorado and California, for example, have allowed recreational use for years, and other states have only approved medical programs. That difference really matters if you're trying to figure out whether you can smoke, vape, or eat it without getting in trouble. From what I've read, the patchwork is more about politics and timing than about the plant itself. My take is that legality is still shifting. I mean, it's a slow shift, but a real one. So I'd say people should pay attention to their own state's rules rather than the whole country. Does that inconsistency feel unfair? To me it just means checking local laws before assuming you're okay.

I've always found it funny that people say the body runs on electricity as if it carries a plug. I don't think it works like a battery or a generator. From what I know, our cells keep sodium mostly outside and potassium mostly inside, and that separation is the real source of voltage. When ion channels open, those ions rush through, and the membrane potential shifts, which lets nerves fire and muscles contract. To me, that's the interesting bit. The body uses ions that are already there, and the heart's regular beats come from cells that start this process on their own.

I keep coming back to a question I have asked myself more than once: how do musicians sample older songs? My answer is that they turn fragments of the past into raw material for new work, and I think that is one of the most human ways to make music. When someone samples an old record, they reach into a specific moment from another era and rebuild it.

A producer usually starts with a short passage. They might isolate four bars of guitar or a short drum break. From there they loop it, chop it into smaller slices, change the pitch, stretch or compress the timing, and layer new drums or synths underneath. That is the craft. The fragment becomes the seed for a new piece.

There is also the legal side, and I think people misunderstand it. A sample often has to be cleared with the people who hold the rights to the old recording. If you use a recognizable piece of someone else's song, you are dealing with the copyright holder rather than the original artist. That can mean paying royalties or getting written permission. Sometimes the fragment has to be reworked until it is unrecognisable. The music business has rules about what counts as a sample and what counts as an independent new composition. I do not pretend the rules are perfectly fair, but they are part of the practice.

What I find most interesting is the listening that comes before the making. Sampling old songs often begins with digging through records, tapes, radio archives, or digital libraries. The search is not random. A producer is looking for a groove or a phrase that fits a new idea. Only small pieces are lifted and reshaped to fit the new track.

For me, sampling is a way of keeping older music alive without freezing it in time. The fragment travels into a new context, and the old song gains a second life. I do not think that makes the original any less important. I think it gives the listener a bridge between eras. A sampled beat is far more than an old tune in a new song. It is a piece of history being carefully reworked, and I find that much more interesting than simply borrowing a melody.

I think it's less about the brain hurting and more about everything wrapped around it. The brain itself doesn't really feel pain, so a headache is usually the pain nerves and blood vessels around the skull sending distress signals. With a tension headache, I'd say the muscles around the head and neck get tight and irritated, and that pressure can build. If you press your temple or the back of your neck while one is on, you often feel that tender spot, which is a clue. It's also common for dehydration or poor sleep to make it worse, because those things make the system around the brain more sensitive. My own take is that the pain is your body's way of saying the wrapping tissues are being squeezed or inflamed, not a message that the brain tissue itself is damaged. The head hurts because the outer structures are under strain.

I can’t even tell if the food is good, since we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, and chose the place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names into their completely useless digital waitlist, and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15! It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait runs that far past payment, just tell people upfront so our night isn't wasted. Absolute disaster, zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. I had figured before going that the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, and afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I expected to pay at one. I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option, but the meat choices were just lamb, prime rib, and chicken, things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. I'd run into Alaskan crab legs at a lot of Vegas buffets, but not rock crab claws, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us, so I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either; it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn't try any. Overall I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles, and if you hit it with the edge of your thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" ends up as "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, usually when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. I finally caught Le Rêve at the Wynn, and I'd call it mixed, maybe a little worse than mixed.

The good part is the circular stage, which is genuinely clever. You're looking down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view, and that's rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, and if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with more clarity.

Clarity is the problem, because I still don't know what the story is. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. There's also way too much happening at once, with too many people and too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. It felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

One ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A couple of friends liked it. If you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, I ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The sales representative got our address wrong because her handwritten “7” was interpreted as a “1.” We meant 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people living there brought it to the local UPS store for return, and after that we didn’t learn about it for several weeks. While we were still in the dispute, we placed another order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two, which I thought was pretty strange. The owner handled it at that stage and admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, but he said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we had not been friendly enough with the residents at 5401, who lived four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and in the end we got a credit.
